sentences.text: Carnotaurus possessed two thick horns above its eyes and a very deep skull resting on a muscular neck.
Large bumps lined the sides of the animal, interrupting the scale mosaic, and there is no evidence of feathers.
The single known individual of Carnotaurus was approximately 7.5 to 8 meters long, making it one of the largest abelisaurids.
Estimates for the mass of Carnotaurus vary across studies, ranging from 1,306 kg to 2,100 kg depending on the method used.
The holotype skeleton of Carnotaurus was discovered in 1984 in the Chubut Province of Argentina within the La Colonia Formation.
The only known skeleton of Carnotaurus was unearthed in 1984 by an expedition led by paleontologist José Bonaparte.
The Carnotaurus skeleton was found on the "Pocho Sastre" farm near Bajada Moreno in the Telsen Department of Chubut Province, Argentina.
José Bonaparte described Carnotaurus sastrei as a new genus and species in 1985.
Researchers suggest the horns and muscular neck of Carnotaurus may have been used for fighting other individuals of its species.
Studies suggest rivaling Carnotaurus individuals may have fought using quick head blows, slow skull pushes, or head-on ramming with horns acting as shock absorbers.
Fernando Novas interpreted several skeletal features in 2009 as adaptations for delivering head blows.
The diet of Carnotaurus is debated; some studies suggest it hunted large prey like sauropods, while others indicate it preyed mainly on small animals.
Carnotaurus is classified as a derived member of the Abelisauridae family.
Carnotaurus is often considered part of the Brachyrostra clade, a group of short-snouted theropods restricted to South America.
Carnotaurus is a well-understood genus within the family Abelisauridae, which was restricted to the supercontinent Gondwana.
In 2009, Juan Canale and colleagues created the clade Brachyrostra to include Carnotaurus but exclude Majungasaurus.
Carnotaurus lived in South America during the Late Cretaceous period, approximately 69 to 66 million years ago.
Carnotaurus lived during the Late Cretaceous, approximately 72 to 69.9 million years ago, in the Maastrichtian stage.
In 2020, Cerroni and colleagues argued that the keratinous sheaths on the horns were not greatly longer than the bony cores.
A 2009 study suggests that abelisaurid arms were vestigial, with nerve fibers reduced to an extent similar to modern emus and kiwis.
Paleontologists do not universally accept the subgroups Carnotaurinae and Carnotaurini.
The specific function of the horns on Carnotaurus is not entirely clear.
